info.text: Questions for Module 4: Latent Factor Models (DSC 428)

name.text: A1: Latent Factor Hypothesis & Factor Axes Interpretation

questiontext.text:
Section A — Question 1 (6 marks)

Explain the latent factor hypothesis and why factor axes should not be interpreted individually.

generalfeedback.text:
Model Answer & Marking Guide:

The hypothesis is that users and items can each be represented as vectors in a shared \(k\)-dimensional space of unobserved characteristics, and that preference is well approximated by the inner product \(p_u^\top q_i\).

Individual axes should not be interpreted because the factorisation is identified only up to an invertible linear transformation: \(P M\) and \(M^{-1} Q^\top\) give identical predictions for any invertible \(M\), so what one run calls a single axis another run may split across two. Interpret the geometry — relative distances and neighbourhoods — rather than named dimensions.

name.text: A2: Three Reasons Classical SVD Cannot Be Applied

questiontext.text:
Section A — Question 2 (6 marks)

Give three reasons classical SVD cannot be applied to a rating matrix.

generalfeedback.text:
Model Answer & Marking Guide:

  1. Missing Data: SVD is defined only for complete matrices, and a rating matrix is overwhelmingly missing.
  2. Zero Imputation Bias: Imputing zeros is not neutral: on a 1–5 scale, zero is an extreme negative assertion about roughly 99% of entries, and the decomposition will expend its limited rank reproducing that assertion rather than the signal.
  3. Mean Imputation Distortion: Imputing means distorts the variance structure and biases factors toward the imputed majority, which also dominates the objective by sheer count.

Resolution Note: The resolution is to optimise squared error over observed entries only, which is no longer an SVD but an optimisation problem.

name.text: A3: Importance of Bias Terms in Matrix Factorization

questiontext.text:
Section A — Question 3 (6 marks)

Why do bias terms matter so much, and what does omitting them cost?

generalfeedback.text:
Model Answer & Marking Guide:

Much of the variance in observed ratings is not interaction at all: it is that some users rate generously, some items are simply good, and the population uses the scale in a particular way. Bias terms \(\mu + b_u + b_i\) model these directly and cheaply.

Omitting them forces the interaction term \(p_u^\top q_i\) to reproduce main effects, consuming capacity that should be modelling genuine user–item affinity, and typically leaves a large fraction of the achievable improvement on the table. In practice, a bias-only model recovers most of the gain over the global mean, so omitting biases is the most common reason a from-scratch MF implementation underperforms a trivial baseline.

questiontext.text:
Section A — Question 4 (6 marks)

Contrast SGD and ALS on convergence, parallelism, and suitability for implicit data.

generalfeedback.text:
Model Answer & Marking Guide:

  • Convergence: SGD makes rapid progress per pass but requires tuning a learning rate and a schedule; ALS needs no learning rate and converges in relatively few iterations, though each iteration is computationally more expensive.
  • Parallelism: SGD updates to shared parameters conflict, making parallelisation awkward; ALS solves each user independently given fixed \(Q\), so it is embarrassingly parallel and suits distributed execution.
  • Implicit Data: SGD cannot enumerate the \(m \times n\) negative pairs and must sample; ALS has a closed form in which the all-pairs term reduces to a precomputed \(Q^\top Q\) plus a per-user correction over observed items, making the full sum tractable.

Takeaway: Use SGD for sparse explicit data on a single machine; use ALS for implicit data at scale.

questiontext.text:
Section B — Question 5 (12 marks)

Perform one full SGD update by hand for:

  • \(\mu = 3.2\)
  • \(b_u = -0.10\)
  • \(b_i = 0.40\)
  • \(p_u = (0.30, 0.10)\)
  • \(q_i = (0.20, -0.50)\)
  • \(r_{ui} = 2\)
  • \(\eta = 0.05\)
  • \(\lambda = 0.1\)

Show the prediction, the error, and all four updated parameters (\(b_u\), \(b_i\), \(p_u\), \(q_i\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Model Answer & Marking Guide:

1. Prediction (\(\hat{r}_{ui}\)):
\(p_u^\top q_i = 0.30(0.20) + 0.10(-0.50) = 0.06 - 0.05 = 0.01\)
\(\hat{r}_{ui} = 3.2 - 0.10 + 0.40 + 0.01 = \mathbf{3.51}\)

2. Error (\(e_{ui}\)):
\(e_{ui} = 2 - 3.51 = \mathbf{-1.51}\)

3. Bias Updates:
\(b_u \leftarrow -0.10 + 0.05(-1.51 - 0.1(-0.10)) = -0.10 + 0.05(-1.500) = \mathbf{-0.175}\)
\(b_i \leftarrow 0.40 + 0.05(-1.51 - 0.1(0.40)) = 0.40 + 0.05(-1.550) = \mathbf{0.3225}\)

4. Factor Vector Updates (using old parameter values on RHS):
\(p_u \leftarrow (0.30, 0.10) + 0.05 \left[ -1.51(0.20, -0.50) - 0.1(0.30, 0.10) \right]\)
\(= (0.30, 0.10) + 0.05 \left[ (-0.302, 0.755) - (0.03, 0.01) \right]\)
\(= (0.30, 0.10) + 0.05(-0.332, 0.745) = \mathbf{(0.2834, 0.1373)}\)

\(q_i \leftarrow (0.20, -0.50) + 0.05 \left[ -1.51(0.30, 0.10) - 0.1(0.20, -0.50) \right]\)
\(= (0.20, -0.50) + 0.05 \left[ (-0.453, -0.151) - (0.02, -0.05) \right]\)
\(= (0.20, -0.50) + 0.05(-0.473, -0.101) = \mathbf{(0.1764, -0.5051)}\)

Marking Note: Full credit requires noting that the prediction was too high (so corrections move parameters down/negatively), and correctly using old \(p_u\) values when updating \(q_i\).

name.text: B6: Implicit ALS vs. BPR and Mziki Recommendation

questiontext.text:
Section B — Question 6 (12 marks)

Explain the difference between implicit ALS and BPR in objective, negatives, and optimiser. For Mziki, which would you choose and why?

generalfeedback.text:
Model Answer & Marking Guide:

  • Objective: Implicit ALS is pointwise—it minimises confidence-weighted squared error between a binarised preference and the inner product, summed over all user–item pairs. BPR is pairwise—it maximises the log-likelihood that an observed item is ranked above a sampled unobserved one.
  • Negatives: ALS treats every unobserved pair as a negative with low confidence, so all of them contribute. BPR samples one negative per positive per update, so most unobserved pairs are never seen.
  • Optimiser: ALS alternates closed-form ridge solves and is parallel per user or item. BPR uses SGD over sampled triples.

Choice for Mziki:
Both choices are defensible if properly justified:

  • BPR: Better fit if the deliverable is a top-\(k\) playlist and the team can afford sampling and tuning, because it directly optimises the ranking objective the product actually exposes.
  • ALS: Better fit if the priority is a stable, easily parallelised model with few hyperparameters over a very large play log, and it also yields item factors usable for similar-track lookups.
  • Production Hybrid Answer: ALS for candidate generation and a pairwise-trained model for re-ranking.

Marking Note: Full marks require a clear choice with a reason grounded in product requirements, not just a technical comparison.

questiontext.text:
Section B — Question 7 (12 marks)

Analyse Soko’s 200-factor failure. Identify both root causes, explain why RMSE improved despite them, and specify the evaluation that would have caught each.

generalfeedback.text:
Model Answer & Marking Guide:

  1. Root Cause One — Capacity Without Data: A 200-dimensional factor vector estimated from four interactions is underdetermined. Regularisation shrinks it, but the residual is fitted noise, so predictions for low-activity users are confident and arbitrary.
  2. Root Cause Two — Silent Architectural Regression: The new pipeline computed factors for all items including brand-new ones, which received near-zero vectors and hence near-zero scores, displacing the content-based fallback that had previously surfaced them. No error was raised because nothing failed programmatically; new items simply never ranked.
  3. Why RMSE Improved Anyway: RMSE is computed over observed test ratings, which are dominated by active users and established items — precisely the region where extra capacity helps. Users with four interactions and items with none contribute almost nothing to the global average RMSE, masking both failures.
  4. Evaluations That Would Have Caught Each:
    • For Root Cause One: Stratified RMSE and ranking metrics computed within user activity buckets (e.g., users bucketed by interaction count), which would show severe degradation in the lowest activity bucket.
    • For Root Cause Two: Tracking exposure share and coverage for items under 30 days old as a standing metric, which would have dropped to near zero on the day of release.

Additional Creditable Points: Implementing a cold-user policy with a minimum-interaction threshold, or reporting results across multiple random seeds since high-\(k\) models are structurally unstable.

name.text: C8: Problem with Zero Imputation Before SVD

questiontext.text:
Section C — Question 8 (2 marks)

Filling missing entries with zeros before SVD is wrong because:

generalfeedback.text:
Correct Answer: (b)

On a 1–5 rating scale, zero is an extreme negative assertion about roughly 99% of entries. The decomposition will waste capacity reproducing that false negative claim rather than capturing the actual rating signal.

feedback.text: Incorrect. While computational cost is a concern, the core theoretical reason is conceptual distortion of ratings.

answer.text: zero is a strong negative claim about most of the matrix

feedback.text: Correct. Imputing zeros asserts a strong negative preference for unobserved entries.
Incorrect. Standard SVD works on rectangular matrices of shape m x n.
Incorrect. Breaking sparsity is a computational consequence, but the main issue is introducing extreme negative bias.

name.text: C9: Tractability of Implicit ALS Sum

questiontext.text:
Section C — Question 9 (2 marks)

In implicit ALS, the sum over all \(m \times n\) pairs is tractable because:

generalfeedback.text:
Correct Answer: (b)

The key property of implicit ALS is that \(Y^\top C^u Y = Y^\top Y + Y^\top (C^u - I) Y\). Since \(C^u - I\) is non-zero only for observed items, \(Y^\top Y\) can be precomputed once for all users, leaving a fast local update over observed items.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Implicit ALS considers all pairs rather than dropping them.

answer.text: the solve factors into a term computed once plus a correction over observed items

feedback.text: Correct. The global Y^T Y is computed once, and per-user solves only add corrections for observed interactions.
Incorrect. While small k helps matrix inversion, it does not solve the m x n summation without the algebraic factorization trick.
Incorrect. Sampling is used in SGD / BPR, not exact implicit ALS.

name.text: C10: Why BPR Beats Pointwise MF on NDCG

questiontext.text:
Section C — Question 10 (2 marks)

BPR often beats pointwise MF on NDCG because it:

generalfeedback.text:
Correct Answer: (b)

BPR (Bayesian Personalized Ranking) directly optimizes a pairwise ranking objective function (maximizing the margin between observed and unobserved items), which aligns directly with rank-based metrics like NDCG.

feedback.text: Incorrect. BPR samples pairs and actually processes fewer item pairs per epoch than full implicit ALS.
Correct. Directly optimizing relative order aligns directly with ranking metrics like NDCG.
Incorrect. BPR uses the exact same matrix factorization parameters (P and Q) as pointwise MF.
Incorrect. Convergence speed is not the primary reason for superior NDCG performance.
